result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.is_simple()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Check if the graph is simple (no self-loops or multi-edges). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L15502-L15590){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.is_simple() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Is simple](/assets/graphs/is-simple.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: four nodes where each pair is joined by at most one edge and no edge loops back to its own node, so is_simple() returns True. Right: the same graph with a self-loop on C and a second, parallel edge between B and D (both shown in the accent color), so is_simple() returns False." width="100%"} A simple graph contains no self-loops (edges from a node to itself) and no multi-edges (multiple edges between the same pair of nodes). edgecase graphs allow both, so this method tells you whether a particular graph happens to avoid them. What counts as "the same pair" depends on directedness: - in a directed graph, `A->B` and `B->A` are different pairs, so having both is fine - in an undirected graph, `A--B` and `B--A` are the same pair, so adding both creates a multi-edge Many textbook results and some algorithms assume a simple graph (for example, the maximum edge count of `n * (n - 1) / 2`, or degree-based measures that would be inflated by parallel edges). Checking `is_simple()` is a quick way to confirm that assumption before running such an analysis. If the graph is not simple, `count_all_loops()` and `count_multi_edges()` show where the problem lies, and `simplify()` can remove the offending edges. The check runs over all edges and ignores the current selection. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if the graph is simple, `False` if it has at least one self-loop or multi-edge. A graph with no edges is simple. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} A single edge between two nodes is as simple as it gets: ::: {#e0cc7546 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B"]) .add_edge("A", "B") ) graph.is_simple() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Adding a self-loop makes the graph non-simple: ::: {#ae9d8b45 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.add_edge("A", "A") graph.is_simple() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` False ``` ::: ::: A multi-edge (a second parallel edge between the same pair of nodes) has the same effect, even without any self-loops: ::: {#0661a5ca .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("A", "B"), # parallel edge, auto-assigned a distinct ID ] ) ) graph.is_simple() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` False ``` ::: ::: Edges in opposite directions are only a multi-edge when direction doesn't matter. The directed graph stays simple, while its undirected counterpart does not: ::: {#b2b01be2 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} directed = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "A")]) ) undirected = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "A")]) ) directed.is_simple(), undirected.is_simple() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: :::
